claims.text: Accelerated coupled degradation is primarily driven by a temperature-dependent shift in the balance between sliding-induced depassivation and thermally activated repassivation.
At 25 °C, passive-film regeneration is too slow to prevent two-body abrasion.
Near 100 °C, a fragile and non-uniform oxide or tribo-layer repeatedly forms and ruptures.
Repeated oxide or tribo-layer rupture near 100 °C causes repeated depassivation events.
Cyclic film disruption combined with minor local Cr depletion accelerates both wear and corrosion.
Near 50 °C, a stable passive film minimizes degradation.
As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 has a lamellar dual-phase microstructure containing approximately 71% L12 and 29% B2.
The B2 lamellae are 2–3 µm wide and contain nanoscale Cr-rich precipitates.
The fine L12/B2 lamellar structure promotes relatively homogeneous Cr availability for passive-film repair.
Homogeneous Cr availability in the lamellar structure enhances repassivation.
At high temperature, intermittent oxide or tribo-layer rupture makes the dual-phase HEA vulnerable to cyclic disruption.
Repeated layer formation and fracture at 100 °C enhances oxidative degradation and third-body wear.
At 50 °C, the HEA will exhibit lower wear volume, lower friction, and a more stable passive film than at 25 °C and 100 °C.
At 100 °C, the HEA will exhibit increased total degradation, higher wear volume, and faster corrosion.
At 25 °C, degradation of the HEA will be dominated by abrasive wear.
The HEA will retain its phase structure better than duplex stainless steel 2205.
The proposed mechanism is limited to 25–100 °C, 5–15 N, 3–9 Hz, a 3.5 mm stroke, and deionized water.
The hypothesis does not claim applicability to continuous service near 1100 °C or to ion-containing industrial environments.
The precise repassivation kinetics and quantitative balance between wear and corrosion remain uncertain and may vary with experimental parameters.
